chapterTitle: Production Metrics with Micrometer and Prometheus

beats.headline: Are you measuring the wrong thing?
beats.subline: Picking the wrong Micrometer primitive creates misleading charts that hide production incidents.
beats.narration: Logs are for debugging, but metrics are for alerting. If you pick the wrong Micrometer primitive, your charts will look healthy while your users suffer. Let's decode the four core types.

beats.title: Counter vs. Gauge
beats.narration: Counters only go up. Use them for completed orders or errors. Gauges track instantaneous values like active connections. Use them for things that fluctuate, but be careful—they can report NaN if the underlying object is garbage collected.

beats.title: Avoiding the Gauge GC Trap

steps.explanation: Micrometer uses WeakReferences. If you pass a local object, the GC wipes it and your metric becomes NaN.
Always back your gauge with a field on a singleton bean to ensure it survives the GC cycle.

beats.narration: Micrometer uses weak references. If you pass a temporary object to a Gauge, the GC will reclaim it, and your metric will silently report NaN. Always back your gauges with a strong reference in a long-lived Spring bean.

beats.title: Timer vs DistributionSummary
beats.narration: Timers track latency. DistributionSummaries track non-time values like cart amounts. Both need histogram buckets to provide accurate p99 data. Without buckets, you are just guessing at your tail latency.

beats.title: Part 1 Locked In
beats.nextPartTeaser: Up Next (Part 2): Why client-side percentiles are a math trap →
beats.narration: That covers the basics. In Part 2, we break down why client-side percentiles are mathematically invalid in a microservice fleet and how to fix it with server-side buckets.

beats.headline: Your p99 is lying to you.
beats.subline: Averages hide tail latency, and aggregating client-side percentiles is mathematically impossible.
beats.narration: Your p99 dashboard is lying to you. If you average p99 values from different pods, you get garbage data. Here is the math behind why that happens.

beats.title: Why Aggregation Fails
beats.narration: Averaging p99s across pods is a classic trap. Pod A handles most traffic, but Pod B's outlier spikes the average. You cannot aggregate pre-computed percentiles. You must aggregate the raw histogram buckets first.

beats.title: Configuring Histogram Buckets
beats.code:
management:
  metrics:
    distribution:
      percentiles-histogram:
        http.server.requests: true
      slo:
        http.server.requests: 50ms, 100ms, 250ms, 500ms, 1s

steps.explanation: Enables cumulative counters per bucket. This allows Prometheus to sum them across the fleet.
Defines the boundaries for your latency targets. Keep the count low to save memory.

beats.narration: Enable histograms in your YAML. This forces Micrometer to export cumulative bucket counters. Prometheus can then sum these buckets across all pods before calculating the true fleet-wide p99 using histogram quantile.

beats.title: True Fleet-Wide p99
beats.caption: Sum buckets, THEN calculate quantile
beats.narration: Always sum the rates of your buckets first. Only after you have the aggregated bucket counts do you pass them into the histogram quantile function. This gives you the true p99 of your entire service fleet.

beats.title: Part 2 Locked In
beats.nextPartTeaser: Up Next (Part 3): How to stop a cardinality explosion →
beats.narration: That's how you get accurate data. In Part 3, we prevent Prometheus from crashing by setting hard cardinality guardrails on your tags.

beats.headline: One bad tag can kill Prometheus.
beats.subline: Unbounded labels like user IDs will cause an OOMKilled crash in seconds.
beats.narration: One rogue tag with high cardinality can crash your entire monitoring stack. If you expose raw URLs or user IDs as tags, you are creating millions of time series. Let's build a guardrail.

beats.title: Enforcing Cardinality Limits

steps.explanation: Limits the unique values for the 'uri' tag to 100. Prevents raw paths from flooding the TSDB.
Drops metrics that exceed the limit, protecting your Prometheus memory head block.

beats.narration: Use MeterFilter to cap your tags. This code limits the uri tag to 100 values. If a scanner hits random paths, the filter drops them and logs a warning instead of taking down your Prometheus server.

beats.title: The Cardinality Formula

nodes.label: Unbounded Tags
nodes.detail: User IDs, Order IDs, Raw URLs

beats.narration: Your series count is the product of all label values. If you add a user ID, you multiply your series count by the number of users. Always normalize your URIs and use enums for tags to keep cardinality bounded.

beats.caption: Find your biggest series consumers

beats.narration: Run these PromQL queries to audit your current load. If you see a metric with thousands of unique label values, that is your next candidate for a MeterFilter or a tag cleanup.

beats.title: Part 3 Locked In
takeaways: Cardinality = Product of all tag values
Use MeterFilter to cap tag values
Never use raw IDs in metric tags

beats.narration: Cardinality is now under control. In Part 4, we define SLOs and error budgets so you can stop alerting on CPU and start alerting on user experience.

beats.headline: Stop alerting on CPU usage.
beats.subline: Alerting on infrastructure symptoms is noise. Alert on user-facing reliability instead.
beats.narration: Alerting when CPU hits 80 percent is useless noise. You should alert when your error budget is burning too fast. Let's define reliability the right way.

beats.title: Symptom vs. SLO Alerting
beats.narration: Stop paging engineers for high CPU. Page them when the error budget is burning. This aligns your team on what actually matters: keeping the service reliable for the user.

beats.title: Multi-Window Burn Alerting

steps.explanation: Checks if the 1-hour trend is burning the budget too fast.
Confirms the spike is still happening. Prevents pages for already-resolved issues.

beats.narration: Pair a long window with a short window. This ensures you only page when there is a sustained burn, not a transient spike that already fixed itself.

beats.title: Error Budget Math
beats.narration: Your error budget is your permission to ship. If you have budget, you ship features. If you burn it, you stop and harden the system. It is the ultimate engineering agreement.

beats.title: Chapter Complete
takeaways: Alert on SLO burn, not CPU
